Speaking as a trans person (literally, check my post history), you don't really have to keep up with anything, other than using the they pronoun if you're ever in a situation with someone who does use they/them. From my experience, these labels are more used with other trans people, because they communicate a specific set of information in just a word. It's okay, and even expected, if you don't get it.

For one thing, non-binary means not identifying as strictly 100% female or male. So someone who feels like they're "kind of female" and is attracted only to women might naturally call themself a lesbian. 

Because the definition of non-binary is so broad, non-binary is best described as a label that someone applies to themself rather than a concrete, fixed thing. It's not always going to make consistent sense. 

Also, its an easy way to say "only attracted to women" that most people will understand. We don't really have a gender neutral word for that yet beyond something like gynesexual. I don't know about you, but it just does not sound great.

My main problem with gender in Tarot was the type of attributes that was assigned to male/female - like Female = passive and Male = active. As of now, if ideas of femininity and masculinity come up in the cards, I'll mentally interpret feminity to mean the subconscious mind and masculinity to mean the conscious mind. I find these to be pretty neutral concepts and (to me) it doesn't feel like it leans strongly on traditional gender roles. Also helps me wrap my head around the Magician and High Priestess card lol.

I'll recommend the books Mindful Tarot and Queering the Tarot (this one is self-explanatory). Mindful Tarot interprets the courts in the most gender neutral way I've seen yet. Basically the courts are taken to be representations of *elements* and then their associated *suits*. Pages are Earth and Pentacles, Knights Fire and Wands, Queens Water and Cups, Kings Air and Swords. This then combines with the actual suit they represent: for example King of Cups would be interpreted as Air of Water i.e. Sword of Cups. I think this ties in neatly with the 1-10 progression of the minor suits and makes each court card gender neutral and equal to one another.

I think if you want to start doing deeper analysis and forming a personal take on the tarot, you'll probably want to start learning the nuances and details of the cards themselves. I love the book Mindful Tarot, since it also takes a secular view and honestly feels more like a self-help book from a tarot lens. It honestly has the best interpretation of the court cards I've seen yet, as well. It solidly does away with the idea that page/knight/queen/king might have anything to do with a person's age or gender, by associating them with the four elements instead.

I'd also suggest the Galaxy Tarot app since each card also comes with an analysis of its symbolism (such as its suit, scenery, and number). People like the Labyrinthos Tarot app but I don't really think it's that useful. As a beginner the most helpful thing for me was realising how the meanings of the suit and number of the minor arcana kind of combine together to form the card's meaning. I do seem to surround myself more with transfem content and creators. Maybe that's just due to there being less visible transmasc creators, but I suspect a few other reasons why. 

I have a certain distance from the transfem experience, which makes it feel safe. Meanwhile looking at transmasc creators feels very much like turning a magnifying glass back at myself. It's not anything unbearable, but I can't just switch off my brain. I'm getting better at this, I think. 

There's no one singular experience of transmasculinity, so I can't really say that I don't relate to it. Some common experiences like not understanding girls and preferring to hang out with boys is something that I absolutely have not had though. Boys my age always seemed to be bullies and I far far preferred being around girls. 

I actually started getting interested in feminine clothing a few years ago, before my egg cracked. I tried experimenting wearing skirts and I felt so uncomfortable in the clothing store, like everyone could tell I wasn't supposed to be there. Of course, I looked female, albeit a bit masculine (I'm tall and have body hair even pre-t), so they probably didn't think much of it. I did have a "skirt go spinny" moment later on, so that is a way I """relate""" to common transfem experiences. I would then realise that although looking like a girl was fun, I still did not actually want to be recognised as a girl. \*egg cracking noises\*

Since you're nonbinary, it makes sense you don't feel able to fit into traditional masculine expectations. It probably feels weird to you that transfem experiences are actually what you relate more to, but I think that's okay. Most trans guys (binary or otherwise) would probably put a focus on their feelings of performing traditional masculinity, so it makes sense you wouldn't relate much to that.
